F1.cap: On the Arduino forum, a voltage divider reads 1.1 V instead of 1.8.

F2.cap: Replies guess: resistor tolerance, the meter, bad solder.

F3.cap: Early on, a reply points to the cause: the ESP32 has no power.

F4.cap: Days later, a test confirms it.

L6.cap: BenchMate gives Muse Spark a bench to run those tests.

L7.cap: An Arduino drives the circuit and measures it. About $40 of parts.

L8.cap: Spark chooses each experiment. I only move the wires.

L9.cap: First, a fault I planted, in a circuit designed for 10 ms.

L32.cap: Spark reads its schematic. I confirm the values.

L10.cap: It measures 21.4 ms. Twice as slow.

L33.cap: Without a bench, Spark guessed: nothing is wrong.

L11.cap: With one, it sees two suspects: a bigger resistor, or a bigger capacitor.

L12.cap: Another step test can't separate them.

L13.cap: So Spark asks for a known load.

L16.cap: Then it passes a waveform it never saw.

L17.cap: Verdict: the capacitor is about twice its design value.

L18.cap: And it says what it still doesn't know.

L31.cap: In the app, every step links back to its raw data.

L19.cap: Spark asks for one fix: restore the designed capacitance.

L20.cap: Its prediction goes to GitHub before I touch anything.

L21.cap: I pull the extra capacitor, and the bench measures again.

L23.cap: Next, a test circuit inspired by that forum problem.

L34.cap: It hides a clamp diode. Spark isn't told the wiring.

L35.cap: Small signals pass. Big ones get flattened on top.

L36.cap: None of the five starting models can do that.

L24.cap: So Spark proposes a new structure: a resistor and a diode.

L25.cap: Its netlist becomes a simulation, then a locked prediction.

L26.cap: Two inputs it never trained on. Both match.

L27.cap: Rules and predictions are locked before each measurement.

L28.cap: Every attempt is kept. Failures included.

L29.cap: Hypothesize. Choose the test. Lock the prediction. Measure. Verify.

L30.cap: BenchMate turns a plausible explanation into a tested one.
